endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: f ) I ndividuals impacted by a payor’s automated decision-making system, including patients and their physicians, must have access to all relevant information (including the coverage criteria, results that led to the coverage determination, and clinical guidelines used).

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Transparency regarding training data, algorithm parameters, and the approval and denial process is essential for maintaining fairness .

endorsements.title: Medicare advantage becoming a disadvantage with use of artificial intelligence in prior authorization review
endorsements.quote: For transparency, state insurance departments or CMS should require insurers to publicly disclose their PA practices, inclusive of denial and appeal rates.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether disclosing automated coverage decision processes, criteria, results, and guidelines to physicians and patients makes denials easier to understand or contest. The recommendation currently rests on two endorsements, one of which uses mandatory language and one of which uses advisory language.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two endorsements reflect expert judgment and do not substitute for measured effects on appeal rates, overturned denials, or patient outcomes.

The Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use state that patients and physicians affected by a payor's automated decision-making system must have access to coverage criteria, determination results, and clinical guidelines. The CHAI Responsible AI Guide describes transparency about the approval and denial process as essential for fairness. Neither document is cited here as binding law or regulation.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare automated coverage determinations issued with and without the specified disclosures and that measure physician and patient understanding of the denial, appeal filing rates, appeal success rates, time to care, and administrative burden on practices. No supplied study documents how often opaque automated denials occur or how often they go uncontested, so the size of the hazard is also unmeasured.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether disclosures written for general audiences would be usable by patients with limited English or low health literacy remains untested, and a health system cannot assume the benefit would reach these groups.
